After the leaves have fallen, we return To a plain sense of things. It is as if We had come to an end of the imagination, Inanimate in an inert savoir. It is difficult even to choose the adjective For this blank cold, this sadness without cause. The great structure has become a minor house. No turban walks across the lessened floors. The greenhouse never so badly needed paint. The chimney is fifty years old and slants to one side. A fantastic effort has failed, a repetition In a repetitiousness of men and flies. Yet the absence of the imagination had Itself to be imagined. The great pond, The plain sense of it, without reflections, leaves, Mud, water like dirty glass, expressing silence Of a sort, silence of a rat come out to see, The great pond and its waste of the lilies, all this Had to be imagined as an inevitable knowledge, Required, as a necessity requires.

# The Plain Sense of Things: Imagination's Confrontation with Its Own Limits

When autumn's leaves have finally fallen, we are left to confront a reality stripped of ornament—stark, unadorned, insistently *there*. It is as though the imagination itself has exhausted its capacity for transformation and retreated, leaving behind a mind that is inert, worn down by its own accumulated knowledge. What remains is not simply an absence of beauty but a kind of exhaustion, a sense that the mind's habitual work of embellishment has, for the moment, ceased.

This blankness resists easy naming. It manifests as a cold, seemingly causeless sadness—a diminishment that cannot be traced to any single origin yet permeates everything it touches. Under its influence, grandeur contracts into something modest and unremarkable: the "great structure" becomes merely a "minor house," its former significance quietly withdrawn. The transformation is not violent but deflationary, as if scale itself had been recalibrated downward.

This diminishment finds concrete expression in the physical world: a greenhouse starved of paint, its surfaces dulled and peeling; an old chimney tilting at an angle that speaks of neglect rather than character. These are not merely incidental details of decay—they become emblems of a larger failure, gesturing toward the repetitive, wearying quality of human existence itself, in which grandeur inevitably erodes into shabbiness, and vitality gives way to entropy.

And yet a paradox emerges at the heart of this apparent bleakness: even the absence of imagination must itself be imagined. To conceive of a world without imaginative embellishment is still an act of imagining—one cannot picture imagination's void without imagination's own participation. The mind, in seeking to strip itself bare, discovers that it cannot fully escape its own creative faculty; even nakedness must be envisioned, and in that envisioning, some residue of imaginative life persists.

This paradox crystallizes in the image of a desolate pond—one emptied of reflections, free of floating leaves, devoid of any stirring life, offering nothing but a bleak and total silence. Even this scene of absolute privation, this vision of ultimate absence, must be imagined into being. It stands not as a failure of imagination but as one of its necessary forms—a stark, inevitable kind of knowledge that the mind must construct even when what it constructs is emptiness itself. The plain sense of things, then, is never simply given; it, too, is an act of the imagination confronting its own limits, and in that confrontation, paradoxically affirming its persistence.

# The Imagination's Necessary Absence: Reading the Paradox of Bare Reality

The poem opens in a register of exhaustion and diminishment, as though the faculties of perception and creation have simply worn out. This is a season after imagination, a landscape stripped of the embellishments that the mind typically layers over the world. The house, once perhaps a symbol of habitation, warmth, and human meaning, has fallen into disrepair—it stands as "reduced," its walls bearing the marks of neglect rather than the ornamental flourishes of a mind actively shaping its environment. Nearby, the greenhouse, an emblem of cultivated growth and controlled nature, has its glass cracked and its panes peeling, no longer sheltering anything alive or verdant. And beside these architectural ruins lies a pond, still and stagnant, its surface offering no reflection of anything beyond itself—no shimmer of possibility, no metaphorical resonance, just water sitting inertly in its basin.

These images work together to construct a vision of late autumn as the season of subtraction. Autumn here is not simply a time of falling leaves and dimming light; it becomes a metaphysical condition, a stripping away of the imaginative overlay that ordinarily transforms mere objects into symbols, mere scenes into meaningful vistas. The bareness of the trees, the starkness of the physical world once its decorative or generative possibilities have been exhausted, seems to offer access to some kind of unmediated truth—the "plain sense of things," to borrow the poem's own governing phrase. In this state, the world appears to reveal itself honestly, without the distortions or enhancements that human consciousness typically imposes upon it. The decaying house is just a decaying house. The pond is just static water. Nothing more.

Yet the poem's deeper and more startling move is to interrogate this very premise. It asks: what does it mean to perceive a world without imagination? Can such a perception ever actually occur, or is the recognition of bareness itself already a creative act? Here the poem turns paradoxical, even self-undermining, in its logic. To notice that imagination has failed, to register the absence of embellishment and the presence of unadorned reality, requires precisely the same faculty that is supposedly absent. The mind cannot simply switch off its capacity to interpret, to shape, to imbue objects with resonance and meaning. Even the starkest desolation, even the most "plain" perception of decay and stagnation, must be conceived, articulated, and held in the mind—and this conceiving is itself an imaginative gesture.

In this way, the poem suggests a profound epistemological entrapment: there is no pure, unmediated access to bare reality, because the very act of perceiving something as "bare" or "real" or "plain" is already an interpretive framework, already a product of the imagination working upon raw sensation. The absence of imagination, then, is not truly an absence at all—it is imagination's own creation, its own necessary fiction. The mind, in trying to strip away its embellishments and arrive at unvarnished truth, ends up demonstrating that it cannot escape itself. Even nothingness, even bleakness, even the starkest winter of the mind, must be imagined into being before it can be known or described.

This paradox gives the poem its philosophical weight and its melancholic, almost circular tone. It does not resolve into a triumphant reassertion of imaginative power, nor does it collapse into despair over imagination's inescapability. Instead, it lingers in the recognition that human consciousness is inherently and inescapably creative, that even our attempts to see things "as they really are," without embellishment or illusion, are themselves shaped by the same faculty we are trying to bypass. The decaying house, the peeling greenhouse, and the stagnant pond are not simply images of a world without imagination—they are proof that imagination persists even in imagining its own defeat, even in constructing scenes of its own supposed absence. The poem thus becomes a meditation on the impossibility of ever truly escaping the mind's shaping presence, revealing that the very concept of "bare reality" is itself one of imagination's most subtle and necessary inventions.
outputs.L5:
# The Silence After

The room settled into stillness, each inanimate object holding its position like a photograph waiting to be developed. A chair. A cup, half-full, growing cold. A window through which afternoon light fell in patient rectangles across the floor.

For hours, nothing moved.

There is something instructive in the way objects wait. They do not anticipate. They do not dread. The vase on the table does not know it is empty of flowers; it simply is, occupying its small allotment of space with perfect indifference to time's passage. After the door closed and the footsteps faded down the hallway, the room did not mourn. It could not. This is the strange gift of inanimate things—they carry no memory of before, no bracing for after.

We are not so fortunate. For us, every after is haunted by what came first. The chair remembers no one sitting in it; we remember exactly who did, and how the light fell then, and what was said before silence took over.

Perhaps this is why we surround ourselves with objects—not because they understand us, but because they don't. They ask nothing. They offer no after that isn't also a continuous now. A book left open to the same page for a week is not being patient; patience implies expectation, and expectation implies a self that persists through time, waiting.

Objects have no such self. They simply remain.

And so, after everything, when we return to a room we've left, it is often the stillness of things that steadies us. The clock, still keeping time. The cup, still cold. The window, still holding its rectangle of light, changed only because the sun has moved—not because anything was lost.

For a moment, standing there, we might envy that kind of permanence: the specific grace of not having to carry what came before into what comes next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic free verse poem about autumn, imagination fading, and an old, decaying house.
counterfactuals.output:
The House at the Edge of October

The house remembers itself
the way an old man remembers his wedding day—
in fragments, in gold light
that may never have been as gold as he recalls.

Leaves collect on the porch
like unanswered letters.
No one comes to sweep them anymore.
No one comes at all.

I used to imagine
that the attic window held a face,
that the crack in the ceiling
was a river on some smaller, secret map,
that the whole house breathed
if you pressed your ear against the wallpaper
at midnight in November.

Now I press my ear against the wallpaper
and hear only my own blood,
insistent, unimaginative,
counting down to nothing in particular.

The maples outside are dying beautifully,
the way everything is allowed to die
if it does so slowly enough,
if it turns orange first,
if it makes a season out of its ending.

I want to be dying like that—
gorgeous, unhurried,
something people stop to photograph.

Instead I am dying like the house:
quietly, from the inside,
the beams giving way
one water-logged winter at a time,
no one noticing until the roof
finally remembers
it was always going to fall.

There was a version of me
that could still find the river in the ceiling crack,
still hear the house breathing,
still believe the attic window
was looking back.

That version is a leaf now,
brown and forgetting its own name,
somewhere in the pile
no one will ever sweep.

The wind moves through the broken pane
like it's trying to remember a song
it used to know by heart.

I stand in the yard
and let the cold say what it needs to say.

I am the house.
I am the leaves.
I am the imagining
that has gone quiet,
gone dim,
gone the way October goes—

not suddenly,
but so slowly you mistake it
for still being summer,
until one morning
you wake up
and everything you loved
is bare-branched,
is letting go,
is already
half-forgotten frost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**The Plain Sense of Things**

After the leaves have fallen, we return
To a plain sense of things. It is as if
We had come to an end of the imagination,

It is difficult even to choose the adjective
For this blank cold, this sadness without cause.
The great structure has become a minor house.
No turban walks across the lessened floors.

The greenhouse never so badly needed paint.
The chimney is fifty years old and slants to one side.
A fantastic effort has failed, a repetition
In a repetitiousness of men and flies.

Yet the absence of the imagination had
Itself to be imagined. The great pond,
The plain sense of it, without reflections, leaves,
Mud, water like dirty glass, expressing silence

Of a sort, silence of a rat come out to see,
The great pond and its waste of the lilies, all this
Had to be imagined as an inevitable knowledge,
Required, as a necessity requires.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of Wallace Stevens exploring the idea that even the absence of imagination must be imagined.
counterfactuals.output:
**Anecdote of the Absent Mind**

Suppose a man who says, *I do not dream,*
who wakes into a room without a color
and calls this room the truth, the plain, the real—

even he must first conceive the plainness,
must dress the bareness in a thought of bare,
must paint the room the color of no color

before he stands in it and calls it empty.
The mind that swears it holds no metaphor
holds, at least, the image of a mind

swept clean, and this is not the broom
but the huge invention of the broom,
the architecture raised to house an absence.

Winter does not know that it is winter.
It is the eye, blue-lidded, half asleep,
that hangs the frost like drapery on the pine

and calls this a season stripped of dream—
as if the stripping were not, too, a robe,
a further weaving of the vacant thread.

Nothing arrives unheralded. Even nothing
comes dressed as nothing, comes announced, comes early
to take its seat among the shapes it claims

it is no kin to. We cannot think the unthought.
We can only think the shape the unthought wears,
walking, if it walked, in what would pass,

if it passed, for weather, or a man,
or a bare room in which someone, still imagining,
folds his hands and says: *there is nothing here—*

and the saying is a lamp he lights to see it,
the supreme and final fiction of the fictionless,
the one bright coin he mints to prove he's poor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
